recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Two reddish galaxies sit side by side at the center, almost encircled by a thin bluish-white ring, with a squiggly blue line just below them. They are a pair of giant elliptical galaxies deep inside SDSS J1531+3414, a dense galaxy cluster in the northern constellation Corona Borealis.

The blue arcs around them are background galaxies whose images the cluster's gravity has bent into streaks. Wound around the two galaxies is something else, a chain of young, blue-white super star clusters 100,000 light-years long, evenly spaced 3,000 light-years apart, twisting like a corkscrew around the cores of the colliding pair. Astronomers first suspected it was another lensed background galaxy, but follow-up work with the Nordic Optical Telescope ruled that out.

The two galaxies are interacting and beginning to share material, and tidal forces from their collision are thought to have shaped the chain. Its even spacing is linked to the Jeans instability, the behavior of gas clumps held together by their own gravity, much like water from a tap breaking into drops.
scale: The corkscrew chain of star clusters is 100,000 light-years long, according to NASA.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and infrared light. F390W is shown in blue, F606W in cyan, F814W in yellow and F160W in red.
understand.eye: Part of the data is infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the colors are assigned to separate filter images rather than recorded as the eye would.

explore: Team leader Grant Tremblay of ESO said the structure cannot last long, perhaps about 10 million years, a fraction of the time galaxies take to merge. Its gas may have belonged to the merging pair, cooled out of the hot plasma around them, or been compressed by a shock wave from their crash. The cluster is one of 23 massive lensing clusters in a Hubble program.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Sees Spiral Bridge of Young Stars Between Two Ancient Galaxies
